items.s: ____ are official papers that give you permission to climb.

tfn.s: Everest is on the border between Nepal and China.
tfn.why: The text says: "Everest is in the Himalayas, on the border between Nepal and China."

tfn.s: All of the ideas that politicians discussed are already rules.
tfn.why: The text says they "should not all be treated as rules already in force".

tfn.s: Guides and rescue teams may have to go back into bad weather to help a climber.
tfn.why: The text says they "may have to climb back into the same thin air and bad weather to bring somebody down".

tfn.s: Most people who try to climb Everest reach the top.
tfn.why: The text does not say how many climbers reach the top.

tfn.s: Supporters think that experience rules would make climbing cheaper.
tfn.why: Critics, not supporters, talk about cost; supporters believe the rules "could cut down the number of avoidable accidents".

focus.note: Small words go with certain verbs and nouns. Learn the whole phrase: pay for, worry about, live on, in the Himalayas.

tfn.s: Waiting in a queue near the summit can use up a climber's oxygen.
tfn.why: The text says a climber held up near the top "is burning through oxygen and body heat".

tfn.s: All the lawmakers support the same experience standard.
tfn.why: The text says "Different lawmakers have backed different standards".

tfn.s: Nepal will pass the bill before the next climbing season.
tfn.why: The text only says the final rules depend on how the process turns out, with no date.

tfn.s: Critics think a previous climb proves that a climber has good judgement.
tfn.why: The text says critics argue that previous climbs "are no guarantee of good judgement".

tfn.s: Fewer permits would help the mountain but would also reduce some people's pay.
tfn.why: The text says halving permits "would certainly ease the pressure" but "would also halve somebody's wages".

focus.note: Check the word before the gap. Verbs like rely, suffer and weigh take a fixed preposition, and so do nouns such as guarantee.

items.s: Many guides rely ____ the climbing season for most of their income.

Any new system has to weigh safety ____ the interests of local workers.

Problems high on the mountain are not limited ____ the climbers themselves.
The leaked report ____ speculation that the government would abandon the plan.
Poor visibility will only ____ the problems for climbers who are already short of oxygen.
A single delay can ____ an otherwise routine descent hazardous.

tfn.s: The writer suggests that the 7,000-metre rule could favour richer climbers.
tfn.why: The text says rules to filter out the unprepared "may end up filtering out the less wealthy".

tfn.s: Headlines saying Everest has been closed to novices are accurate.
tfn.why: The text says the measures were part of a legislative process, not "newly enforceable rules".

tfn.s: Nepali guides have asked lawmakers to cut the number of permits.
tfn.why: The text does not report what guides have asked lawmakers to do.

tfn.s: The writer implies that an earlier climb would not necessarily improve a climber's judgement.
tfn.why: The text says another climb first "is no guarantee of good judgement".

tfn.s: Rules that limit visitor numbers and rules that favour volume would affect guides in the same way.
tfn.why: Fewer visitors would hit guides' income first, while volume would "expose those same workers to avoidable danger".

focus.note: At this level, look for fixed expressions: an adjective plus a preposition (contingent on) or a longer phrase (at the expense of, in lieu of).

items.s: Approval of the permit is contingent ____ proof of prior high-altitude experience.
The commercial interests of operators are often at odds ____ the safety of their staff.
Companies that cut costs ____ the expense of safety invite tighter regulation.
A rule this strict would be tantamount ____ a ban for most amateurs.
A cheaper package may offer extra oxygen in lieu ____ a second guide.

speak.title: Role-play: who should climb Everest?
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: Nepal may ask climbers to prove their experience first. You think this is a good idea because rescues are dangerous for guides. Explain your worries and ask the climber about their experience.

b.text: You've saved for years to climb Everest, but you've never climbed a 7,000-metre mountain. You think the new rule is unfair. Explain why you should be allowed to go, and look for a compromise.

phrases: I'm worried about the risks for the guides.
Have you ever climbed above 7,000 metres?
I've been saving for this trip for years.
That's not fair, because I'm very fit.
What if I did a training course first?
Let's find a solution we're both happy with.
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: did the guide agree to take the climber, and what was the compromise?
